title: Hard exam 2
about: Ten single-choice questions with traps: the wrong PID, a name passed as text, file names with spaces, line continuations, busy mount points and settings that outlive a command.

questions.title: Killing the wrong process
questions.text:
A script was meant to start `sleep 300` in the background and then stop it:
```
sleep 300 &
kill $$
echo done
```
What happens when the script runs?

options.t: `sleep` is terminated and the script prints `done`.
options.why: `kill $$` does not name the `sleep` process.

options.t: Nothing is killed, because `kill` cannot signal a process started with `&`.
options.why: `kill` can signal any process the user owns, in the background or not.

options.t: The script kills itself, so `done` is never printed, and `sleep` keeps running.
options.why: `$$` is the PID of the shell running the script; the PID of the last background command is in `$!`.

options.t: `kill` waits for `sleep` to finish and then ends the script.
options.why: `kill` only sends a signal and returns at once.

questions.title: A name is not a file
questions.text: `notes.txt` has three lines. What does `echo notes.txt | wc -l` print?

options.why: `wc` counts the lines of what arrives on stdin, which is the text produced by `echo`, not the contents of the file.
`echo` outputs one line containing the text `notes.txt`; `wc` never opens the file.

options.t: `3 notes.txt`
options.why: `wc` prints a file name only when it is given as an argument.
`echo` ends its output with a newline, so there is one line.

questions.title: File names with spaces
questions.text: The directory holds `a b.txt` and `c.txt`. What happens when you run `ls *.txt | xargs rm`?

options.t: Both files are removed.
options.why: `xargs` splits the input at blanks, so `a b.txt` becomes two separate names.

options.t: Nothing is removed, because `rm` cannot read file names from a pipe.
options.why: `xargs` turns the names into arguments, so `rm` does run.

options.t: `c.txt` is removed, `rm` complains about `a` and `b.txt`, and `a b.txt` stays.
options.why: The name `a b.txt` is split into `a` and `b.txt`, neither of which exists.

options.t: `a b.txt` is removed, because `xargs` keeps names with spaces together.
options.why: By default it splits on blanks too; `-0` with `find -print0` is needed for that.

questions.title: A line continued
questions.text:
```
cd /tmp; cd /nope 2> /dev/null; \
pwd; echo $?
```
These two physical lines are typed in a shell that starts in `/home/ana`. What is printed?

options.t: `/home/ana` and `1`
options.why: The first `cd` succeeded: the current directory is `/tmp`.

options.t: `/tmp` and `1`
options.why: `$?` is the status of the last command, `pwd`, not that of the failed `cd`.

options.t: `/tmp` and `0`
options.why: The failed `cd /nope` leaves the directory as it was, `;` goes on, and `$?` is the status of `pwd`.

options.t: Only an error, because the backslash cancels the `;` before it.
options.why: The backslash only joins the two lines.

questions.title: Newlines in echo
questions.text:
What do these three commands print, in this order?
```
echo -e 'x\ny' | wc -l
echo 'x\ny' | wc -l
echo -n 'x\ny' | wc -l
```

options.why: Without `-e` the `\n` is two ordinary characters, so there is one line.
With `-e` the `\n` becomes a real newline, so there are two lines.
The third command, with `-n` and no `-e`, prints no newline at all.
The first has two newlines; the second has one (the final newline of `echo`); the third has none, since `-n` suppresses it and `\n` stays as text.

questions.title: A busy mount point
questions.text: A pendrive is mounted on `/media/usb`. In a terminal you run `cd /media/usb` and then `umount /media/usb`. What happens?

options.t: The pendrive is unmounted and the shell is moved to `/`.
options.why: The shell's directory is not changed by `umount`.

options.t: The pendrive is unmounted, and the directory shows what was under the mount point.
options.why: Not while a process still has the mounted filesystem as its working directory.

options.t: `umount` refuses with an error such as "target is busy".
options.why: The shell's working directory is inside the mounted filesystem, which keeps it in use.

options.t: The content of the pendrive is deleted, and then it is unmounted.
options.why: `umount` never deletes data.

questions.title: The empty argument

options.t: `num`, `num`, `other`, `other`
options.why: `5.txt` is matched earlier by `*.txt`: the first matching pattern wins.

options.t: `text`, `num`, `other`, `other`
options.why: With no argument, `"$1"` is an empty string, which matches the first pattern.

options.t: `text`, `num`, `other`, `empty`
options.why: Patterns are tried in order; and `"$1"` with no argument is the empty string, which matches `""`.

options.t: `text`, `other`, `other`, `empty`
options.why: `7z` starts with a digit, so `[0-9]*` matches it.

questions.title: Isolating a target
questions.text: The default target of a machine is `graphical.target`. An administrator runs `systemctl isolate rescue.target` and then `systemctl get-default`. What does the second command print?

options.t: `rescue.target`
options.why: `isolate` changes the state of the running system, not the configured default.

options.t: `runlevel1.target`
options.why: The default is not changed to the runlevel alias either.

options.t: `graphical.target`
options.why: The default target is what the machine reaches at the next boot; `isolate` does not modify it.

options.t: `poweroff.target`
options.why: That is level 0; nothing here asked for it.

questions.title: The path matters too
questions.text: `ana` owns the directory `d` with mode `rw-r--r--` and the file `d/f` with mode `rw-r--r--`. She creates the symbolic link `s` to `d/f`. Which statement is TRUE?

options.t: `cat s` works, because `f` is readable and the link has `rwxrwxrwx`.
options.why: The path to the file goes through `d`, which has no execute permission.

options.t: `cat s` fails with `Permission denied`, although `ls d` still lists the name `f`.
options.why: Reaching `d/f` needs `x` on `d`; the `r` bit only allows listing the names.

options.t: `cat s` fails, because a symbolic link never gives access to a file inside a directory.
options.why: A link works normally when the whole path can be traversed.

options.t: `ls d` fails too, because a directory without `x` cannot be listed.
options.why: Listing the names needs `r`, which `d` has.

questions.title: Who am I
questions.text: `ana` logs in on `pts/0` and runs `su - bob`. In that new shell she runs `whoami`, `id` and `who`. Which statement is TRUE?

options.t: `who` shows a new line for `bob`, because every `su` opens a new session.
options.why: `su` does not register a login session; `who` lists the ones created by logins.

options.t: `whoami` still prints `ana`, because the name of the login does not change until she logs out.
options.why: `whoami` prints the effective user, which is now `bob`.

options.t: `whoami` and `id` report `bob`, while `who` still lists the session of `ana`.
options.why: `su` changes the user of the shell; `who` reads the record of the login, which was made by `ana`.

options.t: `id` shows the UID of `ana` and the groups of `bob`.
options.why: `su -` switches the identity completely.
